scale.source: Wikipedia, "Long and short scales": "Use of the short scale is found in most English-speaking and Arabic-speaking countries"; Wikipedia, "English numerals": the short scale is "always used in American English and almost always in British English". Wiktionary, "billion": "(US, modern British & Australian, short scale) a thousand million".

group_mark.source: English writes 1,000,000.5: the comma groups digits (CLDR 47, en number symbols).

decimal_mark.source: English writes 1,000,000.5: the point marks the decimals (CLDR 47, en number symbols).

space_groups.source: English groups digits with a comma ("1,000,000"); a space between digit strings separates two numbers.

plural_scale_needs_count.source: Wiktionary, "million", numeral sense 2: "(colloquial, hyperbolic) An unspecified very large number". So a plural scale word with no count ("millions of people") names no number, and one with a count ("two million people") does.

scale_noun_agrees.source: An English scale word keeps the singular after a count above one: Wiktionary, "million", usage notes: "Until the early 20th century, million behaved much like an ordinary quantificational noun" ("five millions of pounds"); the modern form is "five million pounds".

joiner_tens_units.source: Merriam-Webster, "twenty-one": tens and units take a hyphen or a space, no "and".

joiner_after_hundred.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": in American English "many students are taught [...] not to use the word and anywhere in the whole part of a number, so it is not used before the tens and ones"; "Despite this rule, some Americans use the and in reading numbers containing tens and ones as an alternative". Both forms read the same.

joiner_between_groups.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": in American English "many students are taught [...] not to use the word and anywhere in the whole part of a number, so it is not used before the tens and ones"; "Despite this rule, some Americans use the and in reading numbers containing tens and ones as an alternative". So "and" between groups is optional.

joiner_before_round_hundred.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). So "and" comes only before a last group below 100 ("two thousand and one"); a round hundred after "thousand and" is no CLDR form.

joiner_before_last_group.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en: %spellout-cardinal writes no "and" ("100: << hundred[ >>];", "1000: << thousand[ >>];") and %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes one before a last group below 100 ("100: << hundred[>%%and>];", "1000: << thousand[>%%and>];", "%%and: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: ' =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": in American English "many students are taught [...] not to use the word and anywhere in the whole part of a number, so it is not used before the tens and ones"; "Despite this rule, some Americans use the and in reading numbers containing tens and ones as an alternative". So a last group joins with or without "and" ("two thousand one", "two thousand and one").

comma_between_classes.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en %spellout-cardinal-verbose writes a comma before a group of a hundred or more after "million" and larger ("1000000: << million[>%%commas>];", "%%commas: 1: ' and =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=; 100: , =%spellout-cardinal-verbose=;"), and %spellout-cardinal writes none ("1000000: << million[ >>];"). Structural, no external source for the choice: in English running text a comma after a number word more often ends a list item, so a comma ends an English number.

ordinal_style.source: CLDR 49 RBNF en %spellout-ordinal: "20: twent[y->>|ieth];", "100: <%spellout-numbering< hundred[ >>|th];". The words before the last are cardinal, so only the last word of an ordinal is ordinal ("twenty-first", "one hundred and first").

decimal_marker.source: "point" names the decimal point ("two point five"). Wikipedia, "English numerals": a decimal is read "as a cardinal number, followed by \"point\", and then by the digits of the fractional part" ("3.1416 is \"three point one four one six\""), and 1.2 million is "one point two million". So a multiplier after the digits multiplies the decimal: "one point two hundred" is 120.

minus.source: "minus" and "negative" before a number make it negative.

minus_idioms.source: No English idiom puts "minus" before a positive number.

article_one.source: "a" and "an" count one only before a multiplier ("a hundred", "a dozen", "a third"); alone they are no number.

of.source: English has no "of" that multiplies a scale word.

fraction_of.source: Orchestrator ruling, knowledge/wiki/plans/number-tagger.md, Rulings: "um terço de dúzia" = 4, a fraction of a collective noun multiplies it; "one third of a dozen" = 4 reads the same in English. Priberam, "dúzia", sense 1: "Conjunto de doze."

denominator_particle.source: English has no particle like Portuguese "avos".

class_noun.source: English names no class with a singular noun after a collective: "tens of thousands" takes the plural.

half_unit.source: In English a half before a unit takes "a" ("half a pound"), so no unit noun follows "and a half" directly.

abbreviation.source: No English number word is also an abbreviation with a period.

lone_decimal_mark.source: The point is the English decimal mark (see decimal_mark). A group mark stands only between digits, so a point right before the first digit marks decimals: ".5" is 0.5. The comma only groups digits, so ",5" is no decimal.

range_cue.source: Wiktionary, "between", sense 1: "In the position or interval that separates (two things), or intermediate in quantity or degree", as in "somewhere between forty and fifty dollars". The "and" joins the two limits, so it ends the first number where the words split into two numbers, the first smaller.
